w1-intro.title: Generative versus discriminative modelling
w1-intro.mustKnow: Know the target distribution each approach represents and what questions it can answer.
w1-intro.coreIdea: Discriminative models predict labels from observations; generative models describe the data distribution or joint distribution so they can sample, score, complete, or condition data.
w1-intro.formulaOrRule: Use P(Y|X) for discriminative prediction and P(X,Y) or P(X) for generative modelling.
w1-intro.commonTrap: Do not call every neural net generative; the model must define or learn a data-generating distribution.
w1-intro.examUse: Start comparison answers by naming the probability object, then list operations: sampling, likelihood, conditioning, missing-data reasoning.
checks: Which probability does a classifier model?
What extra operations does a joint generative model enable?

w1-intro.title: Density, sampling, and inference trade-off
w1-intro.mustKnow: Know that each model family makes different operations easy or hard.
w1-intro.coreIdea: The course is organized around whether a model can evaluate density, draw samples, and infer hidden variables or reverse processes tractably.
w1-intro.formulaOrRule: A good comparison always states density access, sampling procedure, and inference cost.
w1-intro.commonTrap: Do not rank model families by sample beauty alone; exact likelihood and tractable inference may matter depending on the task.
w1-intro.examUse: Use this concept whenever an exam asks you to compare VAEs, flows, EBMs, diffusion, or autoregressive models.
checks: Which models have exact likelihood?
Which models sample iteratively?

w1-intro.title: Conditional generation
w1-intro.mustKnow: Know how a condition changes the probability model and sampling target.
w1-intro.coreIdea: Conditional generation models the distribution of data given side information such as class, text, property, scaffold, or causal intervention.
w1-intro.formulaOrRule: Replace P(X) by P(X|Y=y) or learn a conditional score/denoiser/decoder.
w1-intro.commonTrap: Do not confuse conditioning with post-hoc filtering; conditioning changes the generation distribution.
w1-intro.examUse: Mention the condition variable, how it enters the model, and the trade-off between adherence and diversity.
checks: Give two examples of conditioning variables.
Why is filtering generated samples not the same as conditional generation?

w1-intro.title: Model family map
w1-intro.mustKnow: Know the one-line identity of each major family in the course.
w1-intro.coreIdea: Autoregressive models factorize conditionals; VAEs use latent variables and an ELBO; flows use invertible maps; EBMs use unnormalized energies; score and diffusion models learn denoising directions.
w1-intro.formulaOrRule: Map every model to its distribution parameterization and training objective.
w1-intro.commonTrap: Do not memorize names without knowing the density/sampling mechanism.
w1-intro.examUse: Use the map as the opening paragraph for broad synthesis questions.
checks: Which family uses a partition function?
Which family uses an invertible transformation?

w1-intro.title: Empirical data distribution
w1-intro.mustKnow: Know why the dataset represents an empirical approximation to the unknown data law.
w1-intro.coreIdea: Maximum likelihood and divergence arguments compare the model to the distribution that generated the observed dataset, approximated by samples.
w1-intro.formulaOrRule: Training replaces population expectations with averages over datapoints.
w1-intro.commonTrap: Do not treat the finite dataset as the true distribution without acknowledging approximation and generalization.
w1-intro.examUse: Use this concept when explaining why train/test evaluation is necessary.
checks: Why do we use sample averages in training?
What can go wrong if the empirical distribution is memorized?

w1-mle-lvm.title: Maximum likelihood objective
w1-mle-lvm.mustKnow: Know MLE as the baseline objective for fitting probabilistic generative models.
w1-mle-lvm.coreIdea: MLE chooses parameters that assign high probability to observed samples, turning distribution fitting into optimization of log probabilities.
w1-mle-lvm.formulaOrRule: Maximize the sum or average of log likelihoods over training data.
w1-mle-lvm.commonTrap: Do not maximize raw probabilities directly; products underflow and log turns products into sums.
w1-mle-lvm.examUse: For derivations, write the empirical log-likelihood before discussing approximations.
checks: Why do we use log likelihood?
What parameter is optimized in MLE?

w1-mle-lvm.title: KL divergence to MLE
w1-mle-lvm.mustKnow: Know the algebra connecting distribution matching to log-likelihood.
w1-mle-lvm.coreIdea: Minimizing KL from data to model is equivalent to maximizing expected model log-likelihood because the data entropy term is constant in theta.
w1-mle-lvm.formulaOrRule: Forward KL decomposes into a constant minus expected log likelihood.
w1-mle-lvm.commonTrap: Do not drop the direction of KL; reverse KL has different behavior and is not this derivation.
w1-mle-lvm.examUse: Use this in any question asking why MLE is a sensible learning objective.
checks: Which term is constant in the KL derivation?
Why does KL direction matter?

w1-mle-lvm.title: Latent variable joint model
w1-mle-lvm.mustKnow: Know how hidden variables make a model expressive.
w1-mle-lvm.coreIdea: A latent variable model defines a joint distribution over observations and hidden variables, so hidden structure can explain clusters, styles, causes, or low-dimensional factors.
w1-mle-lvm.formulaOrRule: Specify a prior over z and a conditional likelihood for x given z.
w1-mle-lvm.commonTrap: Do not assume z is observed; if it were observed, learning would be much easier.
w1-mle-lvm.examUse: When asked for a generative story, say sample z first, then sample x from p(x|z).
checks: What is sampled first in a latent variable model?
Why can z improve expressiveness?

w1-mle-lvm.title: Marginal likelihood
w1-mle-lvm.mustKnow: Know why latent variables make likelihood computation hard.
w1-mle-lvm.coreIdea: The observed likelihood requires summing or integrating out z, which is tractable only for special model families.
w1-mle-lvm.formulaOrRule: Compute p(x) by marginalizing the joint distribution over z.
w1-mle-lvm.commonTrap: Do not replace marginalization by plugging in one best z unless the approximation is explicitly justified.
w1-mle-lvm.examUse: Use this as the reason EM, variational inference, and VAEs become necessary.
checks: Why is the log outside the integral a problem?
When is marginalization easy?

w1-mle-lvm.title: Posterior inference
w1-mle-lvm.mustKnow: Know that learning often needs p(z|x), not only p(x).
w1-mle-lvm.coreIdea: Posterior inference asks which latent explanations are plausible for an observed datapoint; many training algorithms need expectations under this posterior.
w1-mle-lvm.formulaOrRule: Use Bayes rule to connect joint, marginal, and posterior.
w1-mle-lvm.commonTrap: Do not confuse the prior p(z) with the posterior p(z|x).
w1-mle-lvm.examUse: Mention posterior intractability when explaining why approximate inference is used.
checks: What is the difference between prior and posterior?
Why does EM need posterior responsibilities?

w2-mle-lvm.title: Closed-book maximum likelihood derivation
w2-mle-lvm.mustKnow: Be able to reproduce the maximum likelihood and KL derivation without notes.
w2-mle-lvm.coreIdea: This repeated deck should be used to make the core derivation automatic: data distribution, KL, constant entropy, log-likelihood objective.
w2-mle-lvm.formulaOrRule: Start with KL and isolate the only theta-dependent term.
w2-mle-lvm.commonTrap: Do not skip the expectation notation; it explains why sample averages appear.
w2-mle-lvm.examUse: Use it as the first paragraph of most probabilistic training answers.
checks: Write the KL decomposition from memory.
Which part becomes the training loss?

w2-mle-lvm.title: Discrete versus continuous marginalization
w2-mle-lvm.mustKnow: Know both forms because lectures use mixtures and continuous latents.
w2-mle-lvm.coreIdea: Discrete latent variables are summed out; continuous latent variables are integrated out, but the conceptual bottleneck is the same.
w2-mle-lvm.formulaOrRule: Use a sum for categorical z and an integral for continuous z.
w2-mle-lvm.commonTrap: Do not mix notation in an answer without saying what type of latent variable is assumed.
w2-mle-lvm.examUse: When comparing GMM, PPCA, and VAE, identify which marginalization form is used.
checks: When do we write a sum over z?
When do we write an integral over z?

w2-mle-lvm.title: Complete-data likelihood
w2-mle-lvm.mustKnow: Know why latent-variable learning would be easier if z were observed.
w2-mle-lvm.coreIdea: Complete-data likelihood treats both x and z as known, often turning hard mixture or latent updates into supervised-style parameter updates.
w2-mle-lvm.formulaOrRule: Observed-data likelihood hides z and requires marginalization or posterior expectations.
w2-mle-lvm.commonTrap: Do not optimize complete-data likelihood on real data unless z labels are actually given.
w2-mle-lvm.examUse: Use this distinction to motivate EM.
checks: What data is missing in observed-data likelihood?
Why does EM use expected complete-data log likelihood?

w2-mle-lvm.title: Approximation bridge
w2-mle-lvm.mustKnow: Know how this lecture points forward to EM and variational methods.
w2-mle-lvm.coreIdea: When exact marginal likelihood or posterior inference is hard, the course introduces lower bounds, approximate posteriors, and amortized inference.
w2-mle-lvm.formulaOrRule: Approximate the intractable posterior or optimize a lower bound on log p(x).
w2-mle-lvm.commonTrap: Do not claim approximation is optional in deep latent variable models; it is usually the central issue.
w2-mle-lvm.examUse: Use this as a transition sentence from MLE/LVM to EM, PPCA, and VAEs.
checks: Why is exact posterior inference usually unavailable?
What is the role of a lower bound?

w2-mle-lvm.title: Latent interpretation caution
w2-mle-lvm.mustKnow: Know that latent variables are useful but not automatically meaningful.
w2-mle-lvm.coreIdea: A latent coordinate can help model density without corresponding to a human-interpretable factor or causal variable.
w2-mle-lvm.formulaOrRule: Interpret latents only when the model, data, or assumptions justify the interpretation.
w2-mle-lvm.commonTrap: Do not equate latent with causal or disentangled.
w2-mle-lvm.examUse: Use this caveat later in causal generative modelling.
checks: Why is a latent variable not necessarily causal?
What extra assumptions help interpretation?

w2-em-ppca.title: EM algorithm
w2-em-ppca.mustKnow: Know EM as alternating posterior inference and parameter update.
w2-em-ppca.coreIdea: EM optimizes latent-variable likelihood by building a bound using current posterior expectations and then maximizing that bound with respect to parameters.
w2-em-ppca.formulaOrRule: Repeat E-step and M-step until convergence.
w2-em-ppca.commonTrap: Do not say EM directly maximizes the exact likelihood in one step; it improves via a bound.
w2-em-ppca.examUse: Use EM whenever the model has tractable posterior expectations but hidden assignments.
checks: What is held fixed in the E-step?
What is held fixed in the M-step?

w2-em-ppca.title: E-step responsibilities
w2-em-ppca.mustKnow: Know what the E-step computes conceptually.
w2-em-ppca.coreIdea: The E-step computes or updates the distribution over latent explanations for each observation under current parameters.
w2-em-ppca.formulaOrRule: For mixtures, this means responsibilities; for general models, expectations under q(z).
w2-em-ppca.commonTrap: Do not update model parameters during the E-step.
w2-em-ppca.examUse: Use responsibilities to explain soft cluster assignment in GMMs.
checks: What does a responsibility represent?
Why is soft assignment useful?

w2-em-ppca.title: M-step expected complete likelihood
w2-em-ppca.coreIdea: The M-step updates parameters as if latent assignments were observed in expectation, using the distribution found in the E-step.
w2-em-ppca.formulaOrRule: Maximize the expected complete-data log likelihood under q.
w2-em-ppca.commonTrap: Do not recompute q inside the same M-step unless describing generalized EM.
w2-em-ppca.examUse: Use this to derive or explain parameter updates.
checks: What objective is maximized in the M-step?
Why are expectations used?

w2-em-ppca.title: ELBO and gap
w2-em-ppca.mustKnow: Know the lower-bound identity behind EM and variational inference.
w2-em-ppca.coreIdea: The ELBO lower-bounds log likelihood; the gap is a KL divergence between the approximate posterior and true posterior.
w2-em-ppca.formulaOrRule: Tighten q in the E-step and improve parameters in the M-step.
w2-em-ppca.commonTrap: Do not call the ELBO the exact likelihood unless the KL gap is zero.
w2-em-ppca.examUse: Use this concept to connect EM, VI, and VAEs.
checks: When is the ELBO tight?
What distribution appears in the KL gap?

w2-em-ppca.title: Probabilistic PCA
w2-em-ppca.mustKnow: Know PPCA as PCA formulated as a Gaussian latent-variable model.
w2-em-ppca.coreIdea: PPCA samples a low-dimensional Gaussian latent, maps it linearly, and adds isotropic Gaussian noise, giving a tractable Gaussian marginal.
w2-em-ppca.formulaOrRule: The covariance is low-rank structure plus isotropic noise.
w2-em-ppca.commonTrap: Do not treat PPCA as ordinary deterministic PCA; it is a likelihood model with noise.
w2-em-ppca.examUse: Use PPCA as the clean bridge from linear latent models to VAEs.
checks: What is the generative story of PPCA?
How does PPCA covariance depend on W?

w3-vae.title: Nonlinear latent variable model
w3-vae.mustKnow: Know why neural decoders increase expressiveness and inference difficulty.
w3-vae.coreIdea: Replacing a linear decoder with a neural decoder lets the model represent complex data manifolds, but usually destroys closed-form posterior inference.
w3-vae.formulaOrRule: Keep the latent prior simple and make p_theta(x|z) flexible.
w3-vae.commonTrap: Do not expect PPCA-style closed-form updates after adding a deep decoder.
w3-vae.examUse: Use this point to motivate approximate inference.
checks: Why does nonlinearity make inference harder?
What stays simple in many deep LVMs?

w3-vae.title: Encoder and decoder roles
w3-vae.mustKnow: Know which network is inference and which network is generation.
w3-vae.coreIdea: The encoder q_phi(z|x) approximates posterior inference; the decoder p_theta(x|z) defines how samples are generated from latent variables.
w3-vae.formulaOrRule: Generate by sampling z from the prior and passing through the decoder.
w3-vae.commonTrap: Do not sample from the encoder when generating unconditional new data unless conditioning on an input.
w3-vae.examUse: Use this to avoid common VAE architecture confusion.
checks: Which network is used after sampling z from the prior?
What does the encoder approximate?

w3-vae.title: VAE ELBO
w3-vae.mustKnow: Know the two-term objective and its interpretation.
w3-vae.coreIdea: The VAE objective trades reconstruction accuracy against keeping the approximate posterior close to the prior.
w3-vae.formulaOrRule: ELBO equals expected reconstruction log likelihood minus a KL regularizer.
w3-vae.commonTrap: Do not interpret the KL term as arbitrary regularization; it comes from variational inference.
w3-vae.examUse: Use reconstruction plus KL language in almost every VAE answer.
checks: What does the reconstruction term reward?
Why is the KL term needed?

w3-vae.title: Amortized inference
w3-vae.mustKnow: Know why a neural encoder is computationally useful.
w3-vae.coreIdea: Instead of optimizing a separate variational distribution for every datapoint, a single encoder network predicts posterior parameters for any input.
w3-vae.formulaOrRule: Inference cost is amortized across the dataset through learned parameters phi.
w3-vae.commonTrap: Do not confuse amortized inference with exact inference; it is fast but approximate.
w3-vae.examUse: Use this concept when explaining why VAEs scale better than per-datapoint VI.
checks: What is amortized across datapoints?
Why can amortization introduce an approximation gap?

w3-vae.title: Reparameterization trick
w3-vae.mustKnow: Know how stochastic latent sampling becomes differentiable.
w3-vae.coreIdea: A Gaussian latent sample is written as a deterministic function of encoder parameters and external noise, allowing gradients to flow through the sample path.
w3-vae.formulaOrRule: Move randomness into epsilon drawn from a fixed distribution.
w3-vae.commonTrap: Do not backpropagate through a raw sampling operation without reparameterization or another estimator.
w3-vae.examUse: Use this for training mechanics questions.
checks: What random variable is independent of phi?
Why does this help backpropagation?

w3-vae.title: Posterior collapse
w3-vae.mustKnow: Know a common VAE failure mode.
w3-vae.coreIdea: A powerful decoder may ignore z, making q(z|x) close to the prior and reducing latent information.
w3-vae.formulaOrRule: Watch for near-zero KL or latents that do not affect reconstructions.
w3-vae.commonTrap: Do not assume a low training loss means useful latent representations.
w3-vae.examUse: Mention decoder strength, KL annealing, or architecture choices as possible remedies.
checks: What symptom indicates posterior collapse?
Why can a strong decoder cause it?

w5-ebm.title: Energy parameterization
w5-ebm.mustKnow: Know how an EBM turns energy into probability.
w5-ebm.coreIdea: Lower energy means higher probability, but probabilities require global normalization by a partition function.
w5-ebm.commonTrap: Do not interpret raw energy as probability; only normalized exponentiated energy is a density.
w5-ebm.examUse: Use this to define EBMs before discussing training.
checks: What does low energy mean?
Why is energy not a probability?

w5-ebm.title: Partition function
w5-ebm.mustKnow: Know why the normalizer is the main computational bottleneck.
w5-ebm.coreIdea: The partition function sums or integrates exp(-energy) over all possible configurations, which is usually intractable in high dimensions.
w5-ebm.formulaOrRule: It makes the density valid but couples every datapoint to the whole sample space.
w5-ebm.commonTrap: Do not ignore Z when deriving likelihood gradients.
w5-ebm.examUse: Use this to explain why EBMs need approximations or MCMC.
checks: What space does Z integrate over?
Why is Z hard for images?

w5-ebm.title: Positive phase and negative phase
w5-ebm.mustKnow: Know the two forces in EBM likelihood training.
w5-ebm.coreIdea: The positive phase lowers energy on data; the negative phase raises energy on samples from the current model distribution.
w5-ebm.formulaOrRule: Likelihood gradients compare data statistics and model statistics.
w5-ebm.commonTrap: Do not train only on data energy; without negative phase the model can lower energy everywhere.
w5-ebm.examUse: Use this for any EBM gradient explanation.
checks: What happens in the positive phase?
Why is the negative phase necessary?

w5-ebm.title: Langevin dynamics
w5-ebm.mustKnow: Know how gradient-based MCMC samples from an EBM approximately.
w5-ebm.coreIdea: Langevin dynamics moves samples downhill in energy while adding Gaussian noise to preserve stochastic exploration.
w5-ebm.formulaOrRule: Iterative updates combine an energy gradient step and a noise step.
w5-ebm.commonTrap: Do not remove the noise term and still call it sampling from the model; that becomes deterministic optimization.
w5-ebm.examUse: Use this to explain why EBM sampling can be slow.
checks: Why add noise in Langevin dynamics?
What gradient is used?

w5-ebm.title: Contrastive divergence and persistent chains
w5-ebm.mustKnow: Know common approximations for the negative phase.
w5-ebm.coreIdea: Because exact model samples are expensive, training often uses short chains, replay buffers, or persistent chains to approximate negative samples.
w5-ebm.formulaOrRule: Approximation quality depends on mixing and chain initialization.
w5-ebm.commonTrap: Do not claim contrastive divergence gives exact maximum likelihood.
w5-ebm.examUse: Use this as the practical training caveat for EBMs.
checks: Why are persistent chains useful?
What bias can short chains introduce?

w5-flow.title: Normalising flow as invertible transport
w5-flow.coreIdea: A normalising flow transports a simple base distribution into the data distribution through an invertible map.
w5-flow.formulaOrRule: Invertibility lets the same model sample forward and evaluate density backward.
w5-flow.commonTrap: Do not use non-invertible arbitrary neural networks if exact flow likelihood is required.
w5-flow.examUse: Use this as the first sentence of a flow definition.
checks: What distribution is transformed by a flow?
Why is invertibility required?

w5-flow.title: Change of variables
w5-flow.mustKnow: Know the exact likelihood formula for flows.
w5-flow.coreIdea: Density changes by the base density times a Jacobian volume correction under an invertible transformation.
w5-flow.formulaOrRule: Evaluate x by mapping it back to z and adding log absolute determinant.
w5-flow.commonTrap: Do not omit the determinant; it is what preserves probability mass under stretching.
w5-flow.examUse: Use this formula for almost every flow derivation.
checks: Which direction maps x to z for likelihood?
What does the determinant correct?

w5-flow.title: Jacobian determinant intuition
w5-flow.mustKnow: Know what the determinant means geometrically.
w5-flow.coreIdea: The Jacobian determinant measures local volume expansion or compression, so density decreases when volume expands and increases when volume compresses.
w5-flow.formulaOrRule: Small regions transform according to the local linearization.
w5-flow.commonTrap: Do not treat the determinant as a generic penalty; it is required by probability conservation.
w5-flow.examUse: Use this to explain the one-dimensional stretch examples.
checks: What happens to density under volume expansion?
Why is absolute value used?

w5-flow.title: Coupling layers
w5-flow.mustKnow: Know why structured layers are used in practical flows.
w5-flow.coreIdea: Coupling layers keep part of the input unchanged while transforming the rest, making the inverse and determinant cheap.
w5-flow.formulaOrRule: Architecture is restricted to keep determinants tractable.
w5-flow.commonTrap: Do not assume any expressive neural layer can be dropped into a flow.
w5-flow.examUse: Use coupling as the standard example of flow design trade-offs.
checks: Why do coupling layers make determinants cheap?
What is the expressiveness trade-off?

w5-flow.title: Exact likelihood versus architectural constraint
w5-flow.mustKnow: Know the main advantage and cost of flows.
w5-flow.coreIdea: Flows provide exact likelihood and efficient sampling, but require invertible transformations with tractable Jacobians.
w5-flow.formulaOrRule: The benefit is mathematical cleanliness; the cost is constrained model design.
w5-flow.commonTrap: Do not conclude flows dominate VAEs or diffusion just because likelihood is exact.
w5-flow.examUse: Use this in model comparison answers.
checks: What is exact in a flow?
What constraints buy that exactness?

w5-flow.title: Conditional normalising flow
w5-flow.mustKnow: Know how flows can be steered by side information.
w5-flow.coreIdea: A conditional flow lets transformation parameters depend on a condition while preserving invertibility with respect to x.
w5-flow.formulaOrRule: Model p(x|y) through an invertible map whose parameters receive y.
w5-flow.commonTrap: Do not make y part of the variable that must be inverted unless the model is designed for it.
w5-flow.examUse: Use this when connecting flows to controlled generation.
checks: What variable remains invertible?
How can the condition enter the model?

w5-score.title: Score function
w5-score.mustKnow: Know the object learned by score-based models.
w5-score.coreIdea: The score is the gradient of log density with respect to the data; it points toward locally increasing probability.
w5-score.formulaOrRule: The model learns a vector field over data space.
w5-score.commonTrap: Do not confuse score with a scalar classifier score; here it is a gradient vector.
w5-score.examUse: Use this definition before discussing score matching or diffusion.
checks: What is the score a gradient of?
Why is it a vector field?

w5-score.title: Normalizer disappears in the score
w5-score.mustKnow: Know why scores avoid partition functions.
w5-score.coreIdea: The gradient with respect to x of a constant log normalizer is zero, so unnormalized densities can still have learnable scores.
w5-score.formulaOrRule: If p is proportional to unnormalized density, the score ignores log Z.
w5-score.commonTrap: Do not say the model has normalized likelihood just because it learns a score.
w5-score.examUse: Use this to connect EBMs and score matching.
checks: Why does log Z vanish?
What remains unavailable even if the score is known?

w5-score.title: Score matching
w5-score.mustKnow: Know the training principle for score models.
w5-score.coreIdea: Score matching fits the model score to the data score without requiring normalized likelihood, often through objectives involving derivatives of the score network.
w5-score.formulaOrRule: Minimize discrepancy between true and model scores.
w5-score.commonTrap: Do not assume the true score is directly observed; objectives are designed to avoid needing it explicitly.
w5-score.examUse: Use this when asked how score models train without likelihood.
checks: What is being matched?
Why is direct true-score supervision unavailable?

w5-score.title: Denoising score matching
w5-score.coreIdea: By corrupting data with Gaussian noise, the model learns directions that denoise samples back toward high-density regions.
w5-score.formulaOrRule: Train across noise levels to cover low-density regions.
w5-score.commonTrap: Do not train only at zero noise and expect robust sampling from random noise.
w5-score.examUse: Use this as the bridge from score models to diffusion.
checks: Why add noise to training data?
How does denoising relate to score estimation?

w5-score.title: Noise conditional score networks
w5-score.mustKnow: Know why multiple noise levels are used.
w5-score.coreIdea: Different noise scales smooth the data distribution differently, allowing the model to learn global-to-local directions.
w5-score.formulaOrRule: Condition the score network on the noise level or timestep.
w5-score.commonTrap: Do not use one score field for all noise scales without telling the model the scale.
w5-score.examUse: Use this to explain diffusion timestep conditioning.
checks: What does large noise teach?
Why provide the noise level as input?

w5-score.title: Langevin score sampling
w5-score.coreIdea: Starting from noise, Langevin updates move along the learned score and inject randomness to sample from the learned distribution.
w5-score.formulaOrRule: Gradient step plus noise step repeated many times.
w5-score.commonTrap: Do not interpret one update as full generation; the chain is iterative.
w5-score.examUse: Use this when comparing score sampling with diffusion reverse chains.
checks: Why is sampling iterative?
What roles do score and noise play?

w6-diffusion.title: Forward noising process
w6-diffusion.mustKnow: Know the fixed process that corrupts data into noise.
w6-diffusion.coreIdea: Diffusion training defines a Markov chain that gradually adds Gaussian noise to clean data until it becomes nearly standard normal.
w6-diffusion.formulaOrRule: The forward process is known and not learned.
w6-diffusion.commonTrap: Do not say the model learns to add noise; it learns the reverse denoising process.
w6-diffusion.examUse: Use this as step one of any diffusion explanation.
checks: Which process is fixed?
What happens as t approaches T?

w6-diffusion.title: Closed-form noisy sample
w6-diffusion.mustKnow: Know why training can sample any timestep directly.
w6-diffusion.coreIdea: The Gaussian forward chain has a closed form that samples x_t from x_0 without simulating every previous step.
w6-diffusion.formulaOrRule: Use alpha-bar to combine signal and noise.
w6-diffusion.commonTrap: Do not confuse x_t with a generated sample; during training it is a corrupted real sample.
w6-diffusion.examUse: Use this formula when deriving the noise prediction loss.
checks: Why is direct timestep sampling useful?
What controls signal-to-noise ratio?

w6-diffusion.title: Reverse denoising process
w6-diffusion.mustKnow: Know what the neural network approximates.
w6-diffusion.coreIdea: The learned reverse model predicts how to move from a noisy sample to a slightly cleaner sample, approximating the reverse of the forward Markov chain.
w6-diffusion.formulaOrRule: Parameterize p_theta(x_{t-1}|x_t) or predict noise/score used in that transition.
w6-diffusion.commonTrap: Do not think generation is one-shot; it is a chain of reverse steps.
checks: What distribution is learned in reverse?
Why are many steps used?

w6-diffusion.title: Noise prediction objective
w6-diffusion.mustKnow: Know the common DDPM training loss.
w6-diffusion.coreIdea: The network is trained to predict the Gaussian noise that produced x_t from x_0, which gives a denoising direction.
w6-diffusion.formulaOrRule: Minimize squared error between true and predicted noise.
w6-diffusion.commonTrap: Do not call this plain autoencoding; the target changes with timestep noise.
w6-diffusion.examUse: Use this to connect practical DDPM training to score estimation.
checks: What is the target epsilon?
Why is timestep input needed?

w6-diffusion.title: Score connection
w6-diffusion.mustKnow: Know how diffusion relates to score-based modelling.
w6-diffusion.coreIdea: Predicting denoising directions at each noise level is equivalent to learning scores of noisy data distributions up to scaling.
w6-diffusion.formulaOrRule: Diffusion packages multi-noise score learning into forward and reverse processes.
w6-diffusion.commonTrap: Do not treat score models and diffusion as unrelated topics.
w6-diffusion.examUse: Use this in synthesis questions linking Week 5 and Week 6.
checks: How does denoising imply a score direction?
Why are noise levels central to both topics?

w6-diffusion.title: Sampling cost and accelerations
w6-diffusion.coreIdea: Diffusion models can generate high-quality samples but often require many iterative reverse steps; deterministic samplers or distillation can reduce steps.
w6-diffusion.formulaOrRule: Quality, diversity, and speed are controlled by sampler and schedule.
w6-diffusion.commonTrap: Do not compare diffusion speed to one-pass models without mentioning number of function evaluations.
w6-diffusion.examUse: Use this in model comparison and deployment questions.
checks: Why is diffusion sampling slow?
What kinds of methods reduce sampling steps?

w6-flow-matching.title: Continuous normalising flow
w6-flow-matching.mustKnow: Know how a flow can be defined by an ODE.
w6-flow-matching.coreIdea: A continuous normalising flow moves samples through time using a learned velocity field instead of a finite stack of invertible layers.
w6-flow-matching.formulaOrRule: The state follows dx/dt equals v_theta(t,x).
w6-flow-matching.commonTrap: Do not think continuous means non-invertible; ODE flows are invertible under standard conditions.
w6-flow-matching.examUse: Use this to bridge discrete normalising flows and flow matching.
checks: What defines the transformation over time?
Why can an ODE flow be invertible?

w6-flow-matching.title: Continuity equation
w6-flow-matching.mustKnow: Know how density changes under a velocity field.
w6-flow-matching.coreIdea: As probability mass flows through space, log-density changes according to the negative divergence of the velocity field along trajectories.
w6-flow-matching.formulaOrRule: Divergence measures local expansion or compression.
w6-flow-matching.commonTrap: Do not use ordinary Jacobian determinant formulas without adapting to continuous time.
w6-flow-matching.examUse: Use this to explain likelihood in continuous flows.
checks: What does positive divergence do to density?
Why is this a PDE/ODE density relation?

w6-flow-matching.title: Flow Matching objective
w6-flow-matching.mustKnow: Know what is supervised in flow matching.
w6-flow-matching.coreIdea: Flow matching trains the model velocity field to match a target velocity along a chosen probability path from noise to data.
w6-flow-matching.formulaOrRule: The loss is regression on velocities, not direct likelihood maximization.
w6-flow-matching.commonTrap: Do not describe flow matching as simply another DDPM loss; the target is a velocity field.
w6-flow-matching.examUse: Use this as the core definition of the lecture.
checks: What is the model predicting?
What does the target velocity represent?

w6-flow-matching.title: Probability paths
w6-flow-matching.mustKnow: Know that different paths define different learning problems.
w6-flow-matching.coreIdea: A probability path specifies intermediate distributions between base noise and data; the velocity field transports mass along this path.
w6-flow-matching.formulaOrRule: Path choice can encode straight-line interpolation, optimal transport, or diffusion-like behavior.
w6-flow-matching.commonTrap: Do not discuss flow matching without specifying what path is being matched.
w6-flow-matching.examUse: Use this to compare conditional flow matching variants.
checks: What are endpoints of the path?
How can path choice affect training?

w6-flow-matching.title: Simulation-free training
w6-flow-matching.mustKnow: Know a key advantage of flow matching.
w6-flow-matching.coreIdea: Flow matching can train on sampled intermediate points and target velocities without simulating the whole ODE during training.
w6-flow-matching.formulaOrRule: This reduces training burden compared with backpropagating through full ODE solves.
w6-flow-matching.commonTrap: Do not claim sampling is simulation-free; generation still follows or solves the learned flow.
w6-flow-matching.examUse: Use this when explaining why flow matching is attractive.
checks: What is avoided during training?
What still happens during generation?

w6-flow-matching.title: Relation to diffusion and optimal transport
w6-flow-matching.mustKnow: Know the conceptual family resemblance and distinction.
w6-flow-matching.coreIdea: Diffusion, flow matching, and optimal transport all move simple noise toward data, but differ in stochasticity, target, and path definition.
w6-flow-matching.formulaOrRule: Diffusion often predicts noise or score; flow matching predicts velocity.
w6-flow-matching.commonTrap: Do not collapse all generative transport methods into one algorithm.
checks: What does diffusion predict?
What does flow matching predict?

w6-evaluation.title: Likelihood evaluation
w6-evaluation.mustKnow: Know what likelihood measures and what it misses.
w6-evaluation.coreIdea: Likelihood evaluates whether held-out data receives high probability, which is important for density models but not always aligned with perceptual quality.
w6-evaluation.formulaOrRule: Use test log-likelihood or bits per dimension only when the model supports density evaluation.
w6-evaluation.commonTrap: Do not compare likelihoods across incompatible preprocessing or supports.
w6-evaluation.examUse: Use this to explain why evaluation needs multiple metrics.
checks: Why can high likelihood samples look bad?
Which model families support exact likelihood?

w6-evaluation.title: Precision and recall for generators
w6-evaluation.coreIdea: Precision asks whether generated samples look real; recall asks whether the generator covers the real distribution and does not miss modes.
w6-evaluation.formulaOrRule: Mode collapse is high precision but low recall.
w6-evaluation.commonTrap: Do not use one visual grid as evidence of coverage.
w6-evaluation.examUse: Use this whenever discussing sample evaluation.
checks: What does mode collapse do to recall?
Can a model have high recall and low precision?

w6-evaluation.title: FID and Inception features
w6-evaluation.coreIdea: FID compares mean and covariance of real and generated samples in a learned feature space, usually Inception features for images.
w6-evaluation.formulaOrRule: Lower FID means generated feature distribution is closer under this Gaussian approximation.
w6-evaluation.commonTrap: Do not use FID blindly outside natural images or with tiny sample sizes.
w6-evaluation.examUse: Use this as the standard image-generation metric explanation.
checks: What statistics does FID compare?
Why can feature extractor choice matter?

w6-evaluation.title: MMD and KID
w6-evaluation.coreIdea: MMD compares distributions through kernel mean embeddings; KID is an MMD-based metric often used for generated images.
w6-evaluation.formulaOrRule: Unlike FID, KID has an unbiased estimator in common settings.
w6-evaluation.commonTrap: Do not interpret a kernel metric without saying which representation and kernel are used.
w6-evaluation.examUse: Use this as an alternative metric when discussing statistical comparison.
checks: What does MMD compare?
Why is KID sometimes preferred to FID?

w6-evaluation.title: Train-test and memorization checks
w6-evaluation.mustKnow: Know why generated samples must be checked against held-out data.
w6-evaluation.coreIdea: A generator can overfit or memorize training examples, so evaluation should inspect nearest neighbours and use held-out splits.
w6-evaluation.formulaOrRule: Compare generated samples to train and test data in feature or domain space.
w6-evaluation.commonTrap: Do not call memorized samples successful generalization.
w6-evaluation.examUse: Use this as an evaluation caveat for every model family.
checks: How can nearest neighbours reveal memorization?
Why evaluate on test data?

w6-evaluation.title: Domain-specific validity
w6-evaluation.mustKnow: Know that metrics must match the data domain.
w6-evaluation.coreIdea: Molecules, proteins, medical images, and causal simulations require validity, constraints, or downstream task metrics beyond image-quality scores.
w6-evaluation.formulaOrRule: Choose metrics that reflect scientific or causal usefulness.
w6-evaluation.commonTrap: Do not use Inception-based FID as proof of quality for non-image scientific objects.
w6-evaluation.examUse: Use this in life-science and causal evaluation questions.
checks: Name one molecule-specific validity metric.
Why is image realism not enough for proteins?

w7-life.title: Need for controllable generation
w7-life.mustKnow: Know why life-science generation is constraint-heavy.
w7-life.coreIdea: Scientific generation needs samples that satisfy properties, structures, functions, and feasibility constraints, not merely plausible-looking outputs.
w7-life.formulaOrRule: Condition or guide the model toward desired biological or chemical properties.
w7-life.commonTrap: Do not equate realistic samples with useful molecules or proteins.
w7-life.examUse: Use this as the opening motivation for the lecture.
checks: Why is plausibility insufficient for molecules?
Name two constraints in protein generation.

w7-life.title: Conditioning mechanisms
w7-life.mustKnow: Know how side information enters a generative model.
w7-life.coreIdea: Conditioning trains the model with labels, properties, structures, motifs, or text so generated samples follow a specified target.
w7-life.formulaOrRule: Model p(x|y) or condition the denoiser/decoder on y.
w7-life.commonTrap: Do not confuse conditioning with selecting after generation.
w7-life.examUse: Use this when describing controlled diffusion or conditional flow models.
checks: What is the difference between conditioning and filtering?
Where can y enter a diffusion model?

w7-life.title: Classifier guidance
w7-life.mustKnow: Know the score modification used to steer diffusion.
w7-life.coreIdea: Classifier guidance adds the gradient of a classifier likelihood to the unconditional generative score, pushing samples toward a target class or property.
w7-life.formulaOrRule: Guided score combines data score and condition score.
w7-life.commonTrap: Do not forget that guidance needs a classifier or property model with gradients.
w7-life.examUse: Use this for derivation questions about controlled diffusion.
checks: What gradient does the classifier provide?
Why can strong guidance reduce diversity?

w7-life.title: Classifier-free guidance
w7-life.mustKnow: Know the practical guidance method without an external classifier.
w7-life.coreIdea: Classifier-free guidance trains conditional and unconditional behavior in one model, then extrapolates between their predictions during sampling.
w7-life.formulaOrRule: Guidance weight controls condition adherence versus diversity.
w7-life.commonTrap: Do not set guidance weight high without expecting artifacts or diversity loss.
w7-life.examUse: Use CFG in modern diffusion control explanations.
checks: What two predictions are combined?
What happens when guidance weight increases?

w7-life.title: Protein representations
w7-life.mustKnow: Know that representation choice is part of the model.
w7-life.coreIdea: Proteins can be represented as sequences, 3D coordinates, backbones, torsion angles, contact maps, or equivariant graphs, each encoding different inductive biases.
w7-life.formulaOrRule: Choose representation according to task: sequence design, structure generation, motif scaffolding, or binding.
w7-life.commonTrap: Do not treat proteins as ordinary image pixels; geometry and invariance matter.
w7-life.examUse: Use this in application questions about biological generative models.
checks: Why does rotation equivariance matter?
When would a sequence representation be insufficient?

w7-life.title: Molecular and protein validity
w7-life.mustKnow: Know the downstream checks required after generation.
w7-life.coreIdea: Generated molecules need chemical validity and synthesizability; generated proteins need stability, structure, and functional plausibility.
w7-life.formulaOrRule: Evaluate with domain-specific constraints and often external simulation or experiments.
w7-life.commonTrap: Do not claim a sample is useful solely because the generative model produced it.
w7-life.examUse: Use this as the safety/scientific caveat.
checks: What makes a molecule chemically invalid?
Why may experimental validation be needed?

w7-causal.title: Causal versus correlational generation
w7-causal.mustKnow: Know why matching observations is not enough for interventions.
w7-causal.coreIdea: A correlational generator can reproduce training patterns while failing when the environment or intervention changes.
w7-causal.formulaOrRule: Causal modelling asks what changes under actions, not only what co-occurs.
w7-causal.commonTrap: Do not call a latent variable causal just because it is interpretable.
w7-causal.examUse: Use this as the motivation for causal generative modelling.
checks: Why can shortcut learning fail out of distribution?
What extra question does causality answer?

w7-causal.title: Pearl ladder
w7-causal.mustKnow: Know the hierarchy of association, intervention, and counterfactuals.
w7-causal.coreIdea: Association observes; intervention sets variables; counterfactuals reason about alternative outcomes for the same unit.
w7-causal.formulaOrRule: Higher levels require stronger assumptions than passive observation.
w7-causal.commonTrap: Do not answer do-operator questions with ordinary conditioning alone.
w7-causal.examUse: Use the ladder to classify exam examples.
checks: What level is p(y|x)?
What level asks what would have happened?

w7-causal.title: Structural causal model
w7-causal.mustKnow: Know the mechanism-based representation of causal variables.
w7-causal.coreIdea: An SCM defines each variable as a function of its parents and independent noise, inducing a graph-factorized joint distribution.
w7-causal.formulaOrRule: Causal mechanisms, not just distributions, support interventions.
w7-causal.commonTrap: Do not infer the graph uniquely from observational density without assumptions.
w7-causal.examUse: Use SCMs to formalize causal generative models.
checks: What are parents in an SCM?
Why do mechanisms matter?

w7-causal.title: Intervention and do-operator
w7-causal.mustKnow: Know why intervention differs from conditioning.
w7-causal.coreIdea: An intervention replaces a structural equation, breaking normal causes of the intervened variable; conditioning merely selects observations where a variable has a value.
w7-causal.commonTrap: Do not write p(y|x) when the question asks about setting x by intervention.
w7-causal.examUse: Use this in any causal effect question.
checks: What equation changes under intervention?
Why can p(y|x) differ from p(y|do(x))?

w7-causal.title: Counterfactual reasoning
w7-causal.coreIdea: Counterfactuals infer the latent/noise state of the observed individual, modify the causal model by an intervention, then predict the alternate outcome.
w7-causal.formulaOrRule: The same unit is considered under a different action.
w7-causal.commonTrap: Do not answer counterfactuals by sampling a new unrelated individual.
w7-causal.examUse: Use the three-step recipe explicitly in exam answers.
checks: What happens in abduction?
Why keep the same latent/noise state?

w7-causal.title: Identifiability and assumptions
w7-causal.mustKnow: Know why causal representations are hard to learn.
w7-causal.coreIdea: Many causal explanations can induce the same observational distribution, so causal factors are not identifiable without assumptions, interventions, environments, or inductive biases.
w7-causal.formulaOrRule: Identifiability is about whether the target is determined by available data and assumptions.
w7-causal.commonTrap: Do not claim disentanglement is guaranteed by unsupervised reconstruction.
w7-causal.examUse: Use this as the main caveat for causal generative models.
checks: Why is observational data insufficient in general?
What extra information can help identifiability?

w7-causal.title: Causal world models
w7-causal.mustKnow: Know how causal structure can help agents reason under actions.
w7-causal.coreIdea: A causal world model represents mechanisms and transitions so an agent can predict effects of interventions and plan beyond observed correlations.
w7-causal.formulaOrRule: Model dynamics with causal variables and intervention-aware transitions.
w7-causal.commonTrap: Do not treat a black-box next-state predictor as causal unless interventions/mechanisms are represented.
w7-causal.examUse: Use this in final application questions linking causality and generative modelling.
checks: How can causal structure help planning?
What would fail in a purely correlational world model?
